query: We are investigating the atomic-scale thermal behavior of AuCoCuNiPt high-entropy alloy (HENA) nanoparticles synthesized via pulsed laser deposition on a silicon nitride membrane. The prevailing hypothesis is that high entropy and sluggish diffusion stabilize the FCC structure against coalescence and segregation. However, in situ heating experiments reveal a progressive loss of sub-5 nm particles and a widening of the size distribution, alongside a reshaping from elliptical to spherical geometries. Theoretical models based on Gibbs free energy often neglect surface energy terms critical for sub-10 nm systems. It has been observed that the FCC structure in these PLD-grown NPs may be governed by kinetic effects rather than entropy. Propose a mechanism explaining why atomic diffusion is surprisingly active in this quinary system, leading to the segregation of specific elements (like Au and Cu) to the surface and subsequent evaporation. Identify the critical temperature threshold where this mechanism becomes dominant, establish the boundary conditions regarding the initial nanoparticle shape (icosahedral vs. truncated octahedron), and formulate a falsification experiment involving simultaneous in situ STEM and atomistic simulations to test if surface energy gradients alone can explain the observed phase separation without invoking sluggish diffusion.

generation.hypothesis: In sub-5 nm AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles, the thermodynamic driving force for surface segregation and evaporation of low-cohesive-energy elements (Au, Cu) is dominated by surface energy minimization gradients rather than configurational entropy stabilization, leading to active diffusion and particle loss at temperatures significantly lower than the bulk sluggish-diffusion threshold.
generation.material_initial_state: Sub-5 nm AuCoCuNiPt high-entropy alloy nanoparticles synthesized via pulsed laser deposition on a silicon nitride membrane, initially exhibiting an FCC structure with elliptical or icosahedral geometries and a compositionally homogeneous bulk.
generation.intervention: In situ heating of the nanoparticles in a vacuum or inert atmosphere within a transmission electron microscope, ramping temperature from ambient to 1000 K.
generation.conditions: Nanoparticle diameter < 5 nm; initial shape anisotropy (elliptical/icosahedral); heating rate 10–20 K/min; background pressure < 10^-6 Pa.
generation.structural_mediator: Surface energy gradients induced by high surface-to-volume ratio and local atomic coordination defects (e.g., edges, vertices in icosahedra) which lower the activation barrier for surface diffusion of specific elements.
generation.mechanism: The high surface energy of sub-5 nm particles creates a thermodynamic instability where the reduction in total surface free energy (driven by the segregation of low-surface-energy elements like Au and Cu to the surface) outweighs the entropic stabilization of the bulk solid solution. This drives rapid surface diffusion and evaporation of these elements, causing particle reshaping (elliptical to spherical) and size reduction, effectively bypassing the 'sluggish diffusion' typically observed in bulk HEAs.
generation.predicted_outcome: A critical temperature threshold (T_crit) of approximately 600–700 K will be observed where the rate of Au/Cu surface segregation and evaporation accelerates exponentially, leading to a measurable loss of particle mass and a narrowing of the size distribution due to the preferential evaporation of the smallest, highest-surface-energy particles. The FCC structure will be preserved in the remaining core but with a compositionally depleted shell.
generation.baseline: The prevailing hypothesis that high configurational entropy and sluggish diffusion stabilize the FCC structure against coalescence and segregation up to temperatures approaching the melting point of the constituent elements.
generation.boundary: The mechanism is strictly boundary-dependent on particle size (< 10 nm) and initial shape; larger particles (> 50 nm) or those with low surface energy facets (e.g., truncated octahedra with dominant {111} facets) will exhibit negligible segregation and remain stable up to higher temperatures, adhering to the entropy-stabilization model.
generation.uncertainty: The exact value of T_crit is uncertain due to the lack of direct experimental data on the surface energy gradients of quinary AuCoCuNiPt systems at sub-5 nm scales; the mechanism assumes that surface energy terms dominate over the entropic term (TΔS) in this size regime, which is theoretically plausible but not yet empirically confirmed for this specific quinary system.

falsification_experiment.design: Perform simultaneous in situ STEM heating and atomistic molecular dynamics (MD) simulations on AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles of varying initial shapes (icosahedral vs. truncated octahedron) and sizes (3 nm vs. 20 nm). The simulations will explicitly calculate the Gibbs free energy change (ΔG) including surface energy terms (γA) and configurational entropy (TΔS) to predict the equilibrium segregation profile without kinetic constraints. The experiment will measure the onset temperature of Au/Cu evaporation and shape evolution.
measurements: In situ STEM imaging of particle size distribution and shape evolution (aspect ratio) vs. temperature
EELS/EDS mapping of surface composition gradients during heating
MD simulation of surface diffusion coefficients and segregation energies for each element
Calculation of the ratio of surface energy reduction to entropic stabilization energy
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis is falsified if: (1) No significant Au/Cu segregation or evaporation occurs below 800 K for sub-5 nm particles, or (2) The MD simulations show that the entropic stabilization term (TΔS) remains dominant over the surface energy reduction term (γA) even at sub-5 nm scales, and (3) The initial shape (icosahedral vs. truncated octahedron) has no statistically significant effect on the onset temperature of segregation, indicating that surface energy gradients are not the primary driver.

Question: How can high-entropy alloy (HEA) nanoparticles be synthesized continuously and scalably directly from pure elemental metal powders without using metal salt precursors?. System: CrFeCoNiMo, CrMnFeCoNi, MnFeCoNiCu, and CrFeCoNiCu high-entropy alloys synthesized from elemental metal powders (Cr, Mn, Fe, Co, Ni, Cu, Mo). Processing: Continuous feed of equimolar elemental metal powders (1.2–2.0 g min⁻¹) into a 45 kW, ~3 MHz induction plasma jet at 66.7 kPa; vaporization in core (>8000 K) followed by rapid quenching (10⁵–10⁶ K s⁻¹) using Ar, Ar-H₂ (8.3% H₂), or Ar-He (77.4% He) plasma gases; collection via cyclone separator and porous filter (2.8 μm pore size). Question: Can high-entropy effects be utilized to induce a significant glass-to-glass transition in metallic glasses, and what are the structural and thermodynamic mechanisms behind this phenomenon?. System: Equiatomic NbNiZrTiCo high-entropy metallic glass (HEMG), with comparative systems NbNiZrTiCu and NbNiZrTiCoCu. Processing: Arc melting of pure elements (Nb, Ni, Zr, Ti, Co, Cu; purity ≥ 99.9 wt.%) under high-purity argon, followed by remelting five times; ribbon production via melt-spinning at a wheel surface velocity of 32 m s−1; heat treatment by heating to 855 K (TA) at 20 K min−1 and cooling at 20 K min−1. Test conditions: Differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) at heating rates of 10–50 K min−1 and Flash DSC at >1000 K s−1; in-situ synchrotron X-ray diffraction from 305 K to 803 K at 30 K min−1; nanoindentation; dynamic mechanical analysis (DMA); atom probe tomography (APT) at 65 K; high-resolution transmission electron microscopy (HRTEM) at 200 kV. Findings: The as-prepared NbNiZrTiCo HEMG exhibits an enormous exothermic peak at 781 K with a heat release of 1.65 kJ mol−1, which is approximately 130% of the subsequent crystallization exotherm (1.27 kJ mol−1).;
